name: OpenAI
warningSignals: Extreme capital intensity of large language model training and inference infrastructure; electricity and GPU supply chain concentration risk
Regulatory uncertainty around AI safety, copyright liability, and data privacy across US, EU, UK jurisdictions
Competitive pressure from well-capitalized entrants (Google, Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic) with existing cloud and distribution advantages
Customer concentration risk; enterprise adoption still nascent and price-sensitive to model performance and cost-per-token economics
opportunitySignals: ChatGPT user base exceeded 100M in Q1 2023; enterprise API adoption accelerating across financial services, healthcare, legal, and software development verticals
GPT-4 release (March 2023) demonstrated multimodal capability and reasoning improvements; pricing power expansion via tiered API and subscription models
Strategic partnerships with Microsoft (Azure integration, $10B+ investment commitment) provide capital, distribution, and cloud infrastructure moat
Potential for licensing, fine-tuning, and custom model deployment to generate recurring revenue streams beyond API consumption

engineOutputs: API token consumption and cost-per-token economics
Enterprise contract value and customer acquisition cost

domainRelevance: OpenAI is the primary architect and commercializer of large language models (LLMs) that are reshaping education, knowledge work, and professional training. ChatGPT and GPT-4 have become de facto reference implementations for generative AI in academic institutions, corporate training programs, and student learning workflows. The company's models are now embedded in educational platforms, tutoring systems, and institutional research infrastructure, making it a critical infrastructure provider for knowledge distribution and skill development.
portalRelevance: OpenAI is a tier-1 anchor in the generative AI ecosystem and a primary signal source for AI adoption, regulatory risk, and capital intensity in technology infrastructure. Its financial structure (private, venture-backed, with Microsoft as strategic investor) and rapid scaling trajectory make it a bellwether for AI commercialization viability, talent concentration, and geopolitical technology competition. Understanding OpenAI's capital requirements, customer concentration, and regulatory exposure is essential for modeling downstream impacts on education technology, enterprise software, and cloud infrastructure demand.

notes.envelopeStatus: PRIVATE — no SEC filings; financial data sourced from news, investor disclosures, and industry estimates only

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: ChatGPT weekly active user metrics and API token consumption (disclosed via blog posts and earnings calls by Microsoft/Nvidia)
Model release cadence and capability improvements (GPT-4 multimodal, reasoning benchmarks, cost-per-token reductions)
Enterprise customer wins and vertical adoption (financial services, healthcare, legal tech integrations)
Regulatory filings and enforcement actions (FTC, EU AI Act compliance, copyright litigation)

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Capital intensity trajectory: estimated $10B+ cumulative spend on training and inference infrastructure (2023–2024)
Revenue run-rate estimation from API consumption, subscription, and enterprise licensing (estimated $1B+ ARR by late 2023)
Competitive positioning vs. Google Gemini, Meta Llama, Anthropic Claude, and Microsoft Copilot ecosystem
Talent and research velocity: publication rate, model release frequency, and researcher retention vs. peers

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Venture-backed cash burn model: high capex, uncertain path to profitability at current pricing; dependency on Microsoft capital commitment
Regulatory inflection risk: EU AI Act compliance, US copyright litigation (NYT, authors), and potential antitrust scrutiny of Microsoft partnership
Customer concentration and price elasticity: enterprise adoption still early; API pricing pressure from open-source alternatives (Llama, Mistral)
Talent concentration risk: key researchers (Ilya Sutskever, Dario Amodei) are irreplaceable; departure would signal strategic instability

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Thesis: OpenAI's regulatory and capital constraints will determine AI adoption pace and competitive dynamics across education, enterprise, and consumer segments
Risk management: monitor EU AI Act compliance costs, US copyright litigation outcomes, and FTC antitrust investigation scope
Hedge positioning: long exposure to GPU/semiconductor capacity (Nvidia, TSMC); short exposure to open-source AI adoption (if pricing pressure materializes)
Engagement strategy: track Microsoft partnership terms, board composition changes, and executive departures as leading indicators of strategic pivots

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Portfolio positioning: overweight cloud infrastructure (Azure, AWS) and semiconductor capacity (Nvidia H100/H200) as beneficiaries of OpenAI capex
Sector rotation: monitor education technology and enterprise software adoption of ChatGPT/GPT-4 APIs; identify winners in vertical-specific AI applications
Hedging: consider long volatility positions on AI regulation announcements (EU, US, UK); track copyright litigation outcomes as binary events
Engagement: quarterly monitoring of OpenAI blog posts, model releases, and Microsoft earnings calls for capital commitment updates and customer concentration metrics

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Quarterly validation: Microsoft earnings calls for Azure AI revenue contribution and OpenAI capex/revenue estimates
Model release cadence: track GPT-5 timeline, multimodal capabilities, and cost-per-token improvements vs. competitive benchmarks
Regulatory outcomes: EU AI Act implementation timeline, US copyright litigation verdicts, and FTC antitrust investigation conclusions
Customer concentration: monitor enterprise customer wins, vertical adoption rates, and API pricing changes via industry reports and customer disclosures

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Model recalibration: adjust capital intensity assumptions based on realized training costs and inference efficiency improvements
Competitive dynamics: reweight open-source AI adoption risk if Llama, Mistral, or other models achieve price/performance parity with GPT-4
Regulatory impact: update compliance cost estimates and timeline based on EU AI Act and US regulatory outcomes
Talent risk: incorporate executive departure signals into strategic stability scoring; adjust valuation multiples based on key person concentration

suppliers.name: Nvidia Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Nvidia H100 and H200 GPUs are the primary compute substrate for OpenAI's training and inference infrastructure. OpenAI is estimated to consume 10,000+ H100 GPUs annually; Nvidia's GPU supply constraints directly throttle OpenAI's model training velocity and inference capacity. The relationship is foundational: without Nvidia's GPU supply, OpenAI cannot scale training or serve API demand. Disclosed via industry reports and Nvidia earnings calls (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Microsoft Azure
suppliers.relationshipNote: Microsoft Azure provides the cloud infrastructure backbone for OpenAI's API services and model training. Microsoft committed $10B+ to OpenAI (2023) and integrated GPT-4 into Copilot, Office 365, and Bing Search. OpenAI's API runs on Azure; Azure's AI infrastructure revenue is now a material growth driver. The partnership is exclusive for consumer/enterprise AI products; disclosed in Microsoft 10-K and earnings calls (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)
suppliers.relationshipNote: TSMC manufactures Nvidia's H100/H200 GPUs and other AI accelerators that OpenAI depends on. TSMC's 5nm and 3nm process capacity is the bottleneck for GPU supply; geopolitical tensions (US-China, Taiwan) create supply-chain risk. OpenAI's capex trajectory is constrained by TSMC's willingness to allocate capacity to Nvidia. Disclosed via Nvidia and TSMC earnings calls, industry reports (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
suppliers.relationshipNote: AWS is a secondary cloud provider for OpenAI's infrastructure; while Microsoft Azure is primary, OpenAI maintains multi-cloud optionality. AWS offers Trainium and Inferentia chips as GPU alternatives; OpenAI has explored AWS partnerships to reduce Microsoft dependency. AWS's AI services (SageMaker, Bedrock) compete with OpenAI's API. Relationship is exploratory rather than committed; disclosed via industry reports and AWS re:Invent announcements (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
suppliers.relationshipNote: GCP provides cloud infrastructure and TPU (Tensor Processing Unit) capacity as an alternative to Nvidia GPUs. OpenAI has explored GCP partnerships to diversify from Microsoft/Nvidia dependency. Google's Gemini LLM competes directly with OpenAI's GPT models. The relationship is competitive rather than collaborative; disclosed via industry reports and Google Cloud announcements (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Anthropic
suppliers.relationshipNote: Anthropic is a direct competitor founded by former OpenAI researchers (Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei) in 2021. Anthropic's Claude LLM competes with GPT-4 on reasoning, safety, and enterprise adoption. Anthropic raised $5B+ in funding (2023–2024) and is pursuing similar API and enterprise licensing models. The relationship is competitive; Anthropic's success signals market viability but also customer acquisition pressure. Disclosed via industry reports and venture funding announcements.

suppliers.name: Meta Platforms (Llama)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Meta released Llama (2023) and Llama 2 (2024) as open-source LLMs, creating price competition and reducing OpenAI's API pricing power. Llama 2 achieved near-GPT-3.5 performance at lower cost; enterprises can self-host or use third-party inference services. Meta's open-source strategy threatens OpenAI's API revenue model. The relationship is competitive; disclosed via Meta announcements and industry benchmarks (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Mistral AI
suppliers.relationshipNote: Mistral AI (founded 2023 by former Meta researchers) released Mistral 7B and Mistral 8x7B models as open-source alternatives to GPT-3.5. Mistral's models are efficient, deployable on consumer hardware, and priced aggressively. Mistral raised €385M (2024) and is pursuing enterprise licensing. The relationship is competitive; Mistral's efficiency and pricing threaten OpenAI's API margins. Disclosed via Mistral announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Hugging Face
suppliers.brainNodeRole: Open-Source Model Hub and Community Infrastructure
suppliers.relationshipNote: Hugging Face operates the primary open-source model repository (huggingface.co) hosting 500,000+ models including Llama, Mistral, and community fine-tuned variants. Hugging Face's Transformers library is the de facto standard for LLM development and deployment. OpenAI's models are available on Hugging Face; the platform reduces barriers to model adoption and fine-tuning. The relationship is symbiotic but competitive; Hugging Face enables open-source alternatives. Disclosed via Hugging Face announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Databricks
suppliers.relationshipNote: Databricks provides data infrastructure (Lakehouse, MLflow) and released DBRX LLM (2024) as a commercial alternative to OpenAI. Databricks' platform is used by enterprises for fine-tuning and deploying custom LLMs. Databricks raised $500M+ (2023) and is pursuing enterprise AI infrastructure market. The relationship is competitive; Databricks enables enterprises to reduce OpenAI API dependency. Disclosed via Databricks announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

suppliers.name: Stability AI
suppliers.relationshipNote: Stability AI released Stable Diffusion (2022) as an open-source image generation model, competing with OpenAI's DALL-E. Stability AI raised $101M (2023) and is pursuing multimodal and video generation. The relationship is competitive in generative AI; Stability's open-source approach mirrors Llama/Mistral strategy. Disclosed via Stability AI announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

logisticsPartners.name: Akamai Technologies
logisticsPartners.brainNodeRole: Content Delivery and API Latency Optimization
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Akamai's content delivery network (CDN) and edge computing services optimize latency for OpenAI's API endpoints globally. OpenAI's ChatGPT and API services rely on CDN infrastructure to serve millions of concurrent users with sub-100ms latency. Akamai's edge computing capabilities support inference workloads closer to end-users. The relationship is critical for user experience; disclosed via Akamai earnings calls and industry reports (2023–2024).

logisticsPartners.name: Cloudflare
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Cloudflare provides DDoS protection, WAF (Web Application Firewall), and API security for OpenAI's public-facing services. ChatGPT and OpenAI API are high-value targets for DDoS attacks; Cloudflare's infrastructure protects against volumetric and application-layer attacks. Cloudflare's Workers platform enables edge-based API rate-limiting and authentication. The relationship is critical for service availability; disclosed via Cloudflare earnings calls and industry reports (2023–2024).

logisticsPartners.name: Equinix
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Equinix operates global data centers hosting OpenAI's infrastructure, GPU clusters, and interconnection points. Equinix's IBX (Internet Business Exchange) facilities provide low-latency connectivity between OpenAI's training clusters and cloud providers. Equinix's capacity constraints directly impact OpenAI's ability to scale GPU infrastructure. The relationship is critical for infrastructure scaling; disclosed via Equinix earnings calls and industry reports (2023–2024).

customers.name: Microsoft Corporation (Enterprise and Consumer)
customers.relationshipNote: Microsoft is OpenAI's largest customer and strategic investor. Microsoft integrated GPT-4 into Copilot (Office 365, GitHub, Windows), Bing Search, and Azure AI services. Microsoft's $10B+ investment (2023) includes exclusive licensing rights for consumer and enterprise products. Microsoft's revenue from AI-powered products (Copilot Pro, Copilot for Microsoft 365) is now material. The relationship is exclusive and foundational; disclosed in Microsoft 10-K and earnings calls (2023–2024).

customers.name: Enterprise Software and SaaS Platforms (Aggregate)
customers.relationshipNote: OpenAI's API is integrated into 500+ enterprise software platforms (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Slack, Notion, Zapier, etc.) for customer service, content generation, and workflow automation. Enterprise SaaS adoption is accelerating; OpenAI estimates 100,000+ developers using the API (2023). The relationship is distributed and growing; disclosed via OpenAI blog posts, earnings calls, and industry reports (2023–2024).

customers.name: Educational Institutions (K-12, Higher Ed, Online Learning)
customers.relationshipNote: ChatGPT adoption in education is widespread; 100M+ students and educators use ChatGPT for tutoring, essay writing, and learning. Universities are integrating GPT-4 into research and teaching; K-12 schools are developing AI literacy curricula. OpenAI's education discount program (ChatGPT Plus for students) drives adoption. The relationship is consumer-driven and policy-sensitive; disclosed via OpenAI announcements and education technology reports (2023–2024).

competitors.name: Google DeepMind and Gemini
competitors.brainNodeRole: Direct LLM and Generative AI Competition
competitors.relationshipNote: Google released Gemini (2023) as a direct competitor to GPT-4. Gemini is integrated into Google Search, Bard, and Google Cloud AI services. Google's research advantage (Transformer architecture, attention mechanisms) and cloud distribution give it competitive parity. Google's pricing is aggressive; Gemini API is cheaper than GPT-4. The relationship is direct competition; disclosed via Google announcements and industry benchmarks (2023–2024).

competitors.name: Anthropic (Claude)
competitors.brainNodeRole: Direct LLM Competition and Talent Drain
competitors.relationshipNote: Anthropic's Claude LLM competes with GPT-4 on reasoning, safety, and enterprise adoption. Anthropic raised $5B+ (2023–2024) and is pursuing API and enterprise licensing. Claude's performance on reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K) rivals GPT-4; enterprises are adopting Claude for risk-sensitive applications. Anthropic's founding team (Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei) left OpenAI, creating talent competition. Disclosed via Anthropic announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

competitors.name: Meta Llama and Open-Source Ecosystem
competitors.brainNodeRole: Open-Source LLM Competition and Pricing Pressure
competitors.relationshipNote: Meta's Llama 2 (2024) achieved near-GPT-3.5 performance at lower cost, enabling self-hosting and third-party inference. Llama's open-source license (LLAMA 2 Community License) allows commercial use, reducing OpenAI's API pricing power. Enterprises are deploying Llama on-premises to avoid API costs. The relationship is competitive; Llama's adoption directly impacts OpenAI's API revenue. Disclosed via Meta announcements and industry benchmarks (2023–2024).

competitors.name: Mistral AI (Efficient LLMs)
competitors.brainNodeRole: Efficient LLM Competition and Cost Advantage
competitors.relationshipNote: Mistral AI's models (Mistral 7B, Mistral 8x7B) are 10–100x smaller than GPT-4 but achieve competitive performance on many tasks. Mistral's efficiency enables deployment on consumer hardware and edge devices, reducing cloud API dependency. Mistral raised €385M (2024) and is pursuing enterprise licensing. The relationship is competitive; Mistral's efficiency threatens OpenAI's API margins. Disclosed via Mistral announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

competitors.name: Cohere
competitors.relationshipNote: Cohere provides enterprise-focused LLMs (Command, Embed) and API services for text generation and semantic search. Cohere raised $250M+ (2023) and is pursuing enterprise customers in financial services and healthcare. Cohere's models are optimized for specific enterprise use cases (customer service, content moderation). The relationship is competitive in enterprise segments; disclosed via Cohere announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
regulators.relationshipNote: The SEC oversees OpenAI's governance and disclosure obligations if it goes public or files as a private company. The SEC is investigating AI-related disclosures by public companies (e.g., Microsoft's OpenAI investment). OpenAI's private status exempts it from SEC reporting, but a future IPO would trigger full disclosure requirements. The relationship is prospective; disclosed via SEC announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

regulators.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
regulators.brainNodeRole: Consumer Protection, Antitrust, and AI Safety
regulators.relationshipNote: The FTC is investigating OpenAI for consumer protection violations (ChatGPT data privacy, terms of service clarity) and potential antitrust concerns regarding the Microsoft partnership. The FTC issued an order (2023) requiring OpenAI to implement safeguards against deceptive AI outputs. The FTC is also examining AI safety and bias in large language models. The relationship is adversarial; disclosed via FTC announcements and news (2023–2024).

regulators.name: European Union (AI Act and Data Protection)
regulators.brainNodeRole: AI Regulation, Data Privacy, and Copyright
regulators.relationshipNote: The EU's AI Act (effective 2024) classifies large language models as high-risk AI systems requiring compliance with transparency, documentation, and safety requirements. The EU's GDPR applies to ChatGPT's data processing; OpenAI faced complaints about GDPR compliance and data retention. The EU is investigating copyright infringement claims (authors, publishers suing OpenAI for training data). The relationship is regulatory; disclosed via EU announcements and news (2023–2024).

regulators.name: U.S. Copyright Office and Litigation
regulators.relationshipNote: The U.S. Copyright Office is investigating OpenAI's use of copyrighted works in training data. Multiple lawsuits (New York Times, authors, publishers) allege OpenAI violated copyright by training GPT models on copyrighted text without permission. The Copyright Office issued guidance (2023) that AI-generated works may not be copyrightable. The relationship is adversarial; disclosed via Copyright Office announcements and litigation filings (2023–2024).

regulators.name: U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
regulators.relationshipNote: NIST is developing AI Risk Management Framework and safety standards for large language models. OpenAI participates in NIST's AI safety initiatives and public comment periods. NIST's framework may influence regulatory requirements for AI systems. The relationship is collaborative but regulatory; disclosed via NIST announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

capitalProviders.name: Microsoft Corporation
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Microsoft committed $10B+ to OpenAI (2023) in exchange for exclusive licensing rights and board observer status. Microsoft's investment is structured as a multi-tranche commitment with performance milestones. Microsoft's capital is critical to OpenAI's infrastructure scaling and R&D. The relationship is foundational; disclosed in Microsoft 10-K and earnings calls (2023–2024).

capitalProviders.name: Thrive Capital
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Thrive Capital led OpenAI's Series C funding round (2023) and is a major shareholder. Thrive Capital is a growth-stage venture firm focused on technology and AI. Thrive's investment values OpenAI at $80B+ (2023). The relationship is investor-founder; disclosed via venture funding announcements (2023–2024).

capitalProviders.name: Khosla Ventures
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Khosla Ventures is an early investor in OpenAI and participated in multiple funding rounds. Khosla is a prominent AI-focused venture firm; its investment signals confidence in OpenAI's long-term viability. Khosla's portfolio includes competing AI companies (Anthropic, others). The relationship is investor-founder; disclosed via venture funding announcements (2023–2024).

capitalProviders.name: Sequoia Capital
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Sequoia Capital is an early investor in OpenAI and participated in Series A and B funding rounds. Sequoia's investment validates OpenAI's business model and market opportunity. Sequoia's portfolio includes competing AI companies and downstream beneficiaries. The relationship is investor-founder; disclosed via venture funding announcements (2023–2024).

executiveTeam.name: Sam Altman
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Sam Altman is OpenAI's CEO and co-founder (2015). Altman previously led Y Combinator (2014–2019) and is a prominent AI entrepreneur. Altman's leadership is critical to OpenAI's strategy, fundraising, and public positioning. Altman's departure or conflict would signal strategic instability. The relationship is foundational; disclosed via OpenAI announcements and news (2023–2024).

executiveTeam.name: Ilya Sutskever
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Ilya Sutskever is OpenAI's Chief Scientist and co-founder. Sutskever is a leading deep learning researcher (co-inventor of batch normalization, key contributor to Transformer architecture). Sutskever's research leadership is critical to GPT model development. Sutskever's departure (2024) to form a new AI company signals potential instability. The relationship is foundational; disclosed via OpenAI announcements and news (2023–2024).

executiveTeam.name: Greg Brockman
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Greg Brockman is OpenAI's President and co-founder. Brockman leads product strategy, API development, and commercial partnerships. Brockman's role is critical to OpenAI's go-to-market strategy and customer relationships. Brockman's leadership of ChatGPT and API products is foundational. The relationship is foundational; disclosed via OpenAI announcements and news (2023–2024).

executiveTeam.name: Mira Murati
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Mira Murati is OpenAI's Chief Technology Officer. Murati leads product development, model releases, and technical strategy. Murati's role is critical to GPT-4, DALL-E, and multimodal model development. Murati's leadership of product roadmap is foundational. The relationship is foundational; disclosed via OpenAI announcements and news (2023–2024).

marketSignals.name: ChatGPT Weekly Active Users
marketSignals.relationshipNote: ChatGPT reached 100M+ monthly active users (January 2023) and 200M+ by late 2023. Weekly active users are a leading indicator of consumer adoption and engagement. ChatGPT's user growth is decelerating (2024) as market penetration increases. The signal is critical for valuation and market opportunity assessment; disclosed via OpenAI blog posts and industry reports (2023–2024).

marketSignals.name: OpenAI API Token Consumption and Pricing
marketSignals.relationshipNote: OpenAI API token consumption is a leading indicator of enterprise adoption and revenue. OpenAI reduced API pricing (2023–2024) to compete with open-source alternatives; pricing power is declining. API revenue is estimated at $1B+ ARR (2023) but growth is slowing. The signal is critical for revenue trajectory and competitive positioning; disclosed via OpenAI announcements and industry reports (2023–2024).

matched.neuralRegionLabel: Striatal Projection Neurons (Cholinergic Interneuron–Mediated Phasic Gating Circuit)

patent.claimDirection: Automated interchange contingency-detection engine that monitors real-time network fee schedule feeds and triggers phasic merchant rate adjustment events within a configurable latency window, analogous to a synthetic TAN pause signal.
patent.noveltyAnchor: Dynamic phasic repricing trigger keyed to network fee effective-date metadata rather than manual billing cycle, with per-vertical interchange qualification scoring to minimize downgrade exposure.

programMatch: NSF Future of Work at the Human-Technology Frontier
grant.angle: Frame as adaptive financial infrastructure research: real-time payment cost contingency learning systems that reduce systemic merchant margin volatility, with the neural habit-rigidity model as the formal dynamical reference.

investment.thesis: Processors with demonstrated interchange optimization automation (real-time qualification scoring, dynamic rate-table patching) will sustain net revenue yield through network fee cycles; those without show lagged margin compression detectable 1-2 quarters post-schedule change—a timing arbitrage opportunity in Shift4 vs. peers.
investment.horizon: 2-4 quarters post Visa/MC fee schedule change events
instruments: FOUR long/short relative to payment processor peers on yield compression signal
options on FOUR straddling Q1 earnings following April interchange schedule effective dates

research.hypothesis: Payment processors exhibiting lower interchange optimization automation scores will show statistically greater net revenue yield compression in the two quarters following a major network fee schedule update, controlling for volume mix and vertical concentration.
research.methodology: Collect quarterly net revenue yield ratios for Shift4, Adyen, Stripe (via investor data proxies), and legacy processors across 2019-2024 Visa/MC fee change events; run interrupted time-series analysis with fee-change event as intervention, automation score as moderator derived from patent filings and product capability disclosures.

knownTreatments: Scopolamine (muscarinic antagonist reducing TAN tonic excitability to restore phasic pause window)
L-DOPA augmentation (restoring dopaminergic D2 modulation of TAN pause probability)
Deep brain stimulation of striatum (exogenous phasic interruption of tonic cholinergic suppression)
